title: Highest-Protein Meats: Ranking per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Meats per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare cooked rabbit, chicken, turkey, beef, lamb and pork by protein per 100 grams and realistic serving.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked lean meats by protein content.

excerpt: Lean cooked meats are closer together than most protein rankings make them look: most fall around 27–33 g per 100 g. Cut and cooking water loss can matter as much as the animal itself.
content_html:
Search for the “highest-protein meat” and it sounds as though there should be one obvious winner. Put comparable lean cooked cuts side by side and the more interesting result is how close they are: most land between about 27 and 33 grams per 100 grams.

That means cut, fat content and water lost during cooking can move the number almost as much as switching from one animal to another.

Lean cooked meats on the same scale

MeatProtein/100 g
Cooked rabbit~33 g
Skinless chicken breast31 g
Skinless turkey breast29.5 g
Lean beef~29 g
Lean lamb~28 g
Lean pork~27 g

Rabbit and chicken lead, but not by a huge margin

Cooked rabbit can reach about 33 g protein/100 g and chicken breast about 31 g. In a 5-ounce / 142 g serving, that is roughly 47 g versus 44 g.

Both are exceptionally protein-rich; a difference of a few grams in a full serving rarely needs to decide the entire meal.

Turkey and beef: similar protein, different extras

Turkey breast and lean beef are both near 29–30 g/100 g. The more meaningful nutritional difference is often elsewhere: lean beef commonly provides roughly 2–3 mg iron/100 g compared with about 1 mg in turkey breast.

It is a useful reminder that a one-nutrient ranking cannot summarize a whole food.

Lean pork is much closer to poultry than its reputation suggests

Lean pork loin or tenderloin is around 27 g/100 g. Calling “pork” fatty as a category hides an enormous range.

Bacon can exceed 40–50 g fat/100 g while tenderloin may be near 5 g. Same animal, completely different cuts.

Why cooking makes meat look more protein-dense

Raw chicken breast may be around 22–23 g protein/100 g and cooked breast about 31 g. No new protein appears; water leaves.

If 120 g of raw meat containing 27 g protein finishes at 90 g after cooking, those same 27 g are now concentrated into less weight. Raw-versus-cooked comparisons can therefore create artificial “winners.”

Dried and cured meats can win by losing water

Jerky and cured ham may exceed fresh cooked meat in protein per 100 g because much of their water has been removed. Sodium becomes concentrated too.

A dried meat can therefore post an impressive protein number while being nutritionally very different from a fresh cooked steak.

What a normal serving contributes

Meat5 oz / 142 g cooked
Rabbit~47 g protein
Chicken44 g
Turkey42 g
Lean beef~41 g
Lean pork~38 g

On the plate, every one of these is a substantial protein source. The spread between top and bottom is meaningful, but nowhere near the kind of difference implied by calling one meat “high protein” and another not.

What else deserves a look

Fat varies dramatically by cut; red meat generally provides more iron; fresh unsalted meat is low in sodium while many processed meats are high. Sausage, deli meat and a fresh loin are not interchangeable just because they come from the same animal.

The practical takeaway

Rabbit and chicken breast sit near the top, but turkey, beef, lamb and lean pork remain close. Choosing a lean cut and varying protein sources usually matters more than chasing a two- or three-gram edge.

faq.question: Which meat has the most protein?
faq.answer: Among lean cooked meats, rabbit can be around 33 g/100 g and chicken breast about 31 g/100 g.

faq.question: Does chicken have more protein than beef?
faq.answer: Chicken breast is about 31 g/100 g and many lean beef cuts around 29 g, so the difference is small.

faq.question: Why does cooked meat show more protein?
faq.answer: Cooking removes water and concentrates the existing protein into less total weight.
